statement

The same critique describes a US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, without giving its timing measure or adjustment (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018).

The same critique describes a US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, without giving its timing measure or adjustment (Marks & Clark, 2018); read in full, the survey shows a much smaller difference, and the critique misreports both the difference and the sample. In NESARC 2001–2002 (43,093 US adults interviewed once, response 81%), the comparison was restricted to the 2,080 men and 1,217 women (3,297 in all) who had ever had DSM-IV cannabis abuse or dependence: they had first used cannabis at the same average age (16.71 against 16.73 years) and the disorder had begun at similar ages (19.34 against 18.98 years, not significant), and the recalled time from first use to the disorder was 2.64 years in men and 2.24 in women, a difference of 0.40 years, about 5 months (p = 0.026). The comparison was adjusted neither for current age, although the women with the disorder were younger, nor for anything else; it was one of about 50 comparisons made without correction (editors' count on the study card); and it describes speed among people who developed the disorder, not who develops it: the authors cite another analysis of the same survey in which 11.8% of men and 5.4% of women had ever had the disorder. The authors present the 0.40 years as evidence of telescoping outside treatment (Khan et al., 2013).
statement
Randall et al. (1999), a treatment-sample study that the papers read describe in opposite ways, is not yet read.

The treatment-sample study that the papers above describe in opposite ways, read in full, compared people entering a US alcohol treatment trial (Project MATCH, 1991–1993, nine sites; 379 women and 1,210 men with all four landmark ages, recalled at entry; women and men compared within study arm and fifth of current age, nothing else adjusted for): women recalled first getting drunk regularly, first alcohol problems and first difficulty stopping drinking 2.5 to 3.9 years later than men (getting drunk regularly at 26.6 against 22.7 years on average) but reached their worst period of drinking at the same age (35.2 against 35.0 years). The recalled intervals were shorter in women from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 against 2.3 years) and from loss of control to the worst period (5.5 against 7.8 years), not from first problems to loss of control (2.3 against 2.2 years), and, among the 735 people for whom the trial was their first treatment, from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 against 15.8 years). Gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance; the differences were small or absent in the youngest fifth of participants (average age 26.6; getting drunk regularly at 18.8 against 18.0 years) and grew with age; and only 53% of participants reported the landmarks in the order the intervals assume. Women and men entered treatment at about the same ages (38 to 42 years on average), so a later start in women by itself shortens every interval that ends at treatment: women started getting drunk regularly 3.9 years later than men and reached first treatment 4.2 years sooner after that (editors' comparison), and in the editors' approximate reading of the paper's figure the gaps in time to treatment by age group (about 0.8 to 7.7 years) track the gaps in the age of getting drunk regularly (0.8 to 7.1 years). The authors call telescoping relatively robust in people seeking treatment and recommend alerting women in general that they are more likely to develop alcohol problems rapidly (Randall et al., 1999); the papers that cite the study as showing telescoping, and the critique that counts it among studies with fewer telescoping effects, are each partly right.

plain
A US survey about cannabis, known here only from another paper's short description, found a faster course in women.

In a big US survey, among people who had had a cannabis use disorder, women and men had started cannabis at the same age, about 17, and the women's disorder began on average about 5 months sooner after their first use (2.2 against 2.6 years); a review reported this as 2.5 years, which is wrong. In a US alcohol treatment study, women started getting drunk regularly about 4 years later than men but reached their worst drinking at the same age, about 35, so the steps in between looked shorter; the differences were small and grew with age, and because women and men came into treatment at about the same age, a later start alone makes the time to treatment look shorter.

debate.evidence_yes

A US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) is described as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, which is evidence from outside treatment; its timing measure and adjustment are not given and it is not read here (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018; a narrative review's citation for cannabis points to a different paper).

In the treatment sample most often cited, read in full (Project MATCH, 1991–1993; 379 women and 1,210 men entering alcohol treatment), women recalled shorter intervals from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 against 2.3 years) and from loss of control to their worst period of drinking (5.5 against 7.8 years), and, among people in their first treatment, from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 against 15.8 years); the authors call telescoping relatively robust in people seeking treatment (Randall et al., 1999). Outside treatment, in a US general-population survey (NESARC 2001–2002), among the 2,080 men and 1,217 women who had ever had a cannabis use disorder, the recalled time from first use to the disorder was shorter in women (2.24 against 2.64 years, p = 0.026), which the authors present as telescoping (Khan et al., 2013; a narrative review's citation for cannabis points to a different paper).

Evidence is insufficient to say whether drinking at a young age causes alcohol problems in adulthood, or whether the same family, genetic and personal factors lead to both. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected people took part), the 27,616 adults who had ever drunk were asked how old they were when they first started drinking, not counting tastes or sips: lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence was reported by 40.6% to 47.3% of those who recalled starting at 14 or younger, 16.6% of those who started at 18 and 7.9% of those who started at 25 or older (with a rise to 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24), and lifetime abuse without dependence by up to 13.8% (a first drink at 14) against 2.5% (25 or older). After adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history of alcoholism, duration of drinking and current or former drinking, the odds of lifetime dependence were 14% lower, and of abuse 8% lower, for each later year of the first drink, with no confidence intervals or unadjusted estimates given. The age of the first drink was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses, often decades later; conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, family environment and other drug use were not measured; two of the adjustments (current or former drinking, and the duration of drinking up to the last drink) may themselves follow from the disorder; and people who had died, were in institutions or were homeless were not sampled. The authors call the age of the first drink a powerful predictor and ages 16 and younger a particularly vulnerable period, but their closing paragraph says that the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors may explain the link and that a prospective study is needed to tell (Grant & Dawson, 1997). Does drinking young lead to alcohol problems later? This is not known.

Does drinking young lead to alcohol problems later? This is not known. In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who remembered starting to drink at 14 or younger had had alcohol dependence at some time, against 8 in 100 of those who started at 25 or older; but they were remembering back many years, and the survey could not tell whether early drinking itself, or something that leads to both, explains the link.

grade.reasoning
Grant & Dawson (1998), on age at first drug use, is not yet read; the alcohol landmark from the same survey (Grant & Dawson, 1997) has no reference record in the library.

Grant & Dawson (1997), the cross-sectional survey usually cited as the starting point, read in full, adds a steep association between a recalled early first drink and lifetime dependence (40.6% to 47.3% for a first drink at 14 or younger against 7.9% at 25 or older; 14% lower adjusted odds per later year); it describes what US adults reported in 1992 but cannot separate cause from shared liability, as its authors say, so the certainty about cause does not change. The same survey's analysis for other drugs (Grant & Dawson, 1998) is in the answer on starting drugs young.
debate.evidence_yes
In the Seattle cohort, a first drink before 11

In a 1992 US national survey of 27,616 adults who had ever drunk, lifetime alcohol dependence was reported by 40.6% to 47.3% of those who recalled a first drink at 14 or younger against 7.9% of those who started at 25 or older, and the odds of dependence were 14% lower for each later year of starting after adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history of alcoholism, duration of drinking and current or former drinking (Grant & Dawson, 1997). debate.evidence_no
and the review's authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014).

and the review's authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). The authors of the 1992 survey themselves say that other factors associated with an early start more likely explain its link with later disorders, and call for a prospective study to tell whether an early start is a risk factor that can be changed or a marker (Grant & Dawson, 1997).
debate.neither_can_show
No randomized evidence exists, since the age of a first drink cannot be assigned at random.

No randomized evidence exists, since the age of a first drink cannot be assigned at random. A survey that asks adults to recall their first drink in the same interview as their diagnoses can show how strong the association is in the population surveyed, but not what causes it, and it misses people who died, were in institutions or were homeless.
debate.editors_reading
An earlier first drink goes with more adult drinking in several cohorts, and part of that link
An earlier first drink goes with much more lifetime alcohol dependence in a large US survey that relied on recall, and with more adult drinking in several cohorts, and part of that link

evidence_add.locator: Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 104); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 106); column heads of Tables 1 and 2 (p. 107)
evidence_add.extracted: General-population sample: NLAES 1992, face-to-face Census Bureau interviews with 42,862 US adults aged 18 and older in the noninstitutionalized population; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents took part. The analysis used the 27,616 current (18,352) and former (9,264) drinkers: 13,990 men and 13,626 women.
evidence_add.located_by: AI reader 323 (claim writer), from AI reader 304's study card

evidence_add.locator: Method › Measures, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence_add.extracted: Age at first drink: one recalled question (how old the respondent was on first starting to drink, not counting small tastes or sips), test-retest reliability 0.72, asked in the same interview as the lifetime DSM-IV diagnoses (AUDADIS; reliability 0.76 for past-year and 0.73 for earlier diagnoses); abuse counted only in people without lifetime dependence. Duration of drinking ran from the first drink to the last drink (former drinkers) or to the interview (current drinkers).
